Predict one human monetary allocation in an online experiment with US residents. In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.
The displayed response slider is moved with left/right arrow keys and confirmed with Enter. The split changes in USD0.10 increments, from giving nothing to giving the full USD1. Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position. In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.
The displayed response slider is moved with left/right arrow keys and confirmed with Enter. The split changes in USD0.10 increments, from giving nothing to giving the full USD1. Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position. Predict the amount GIVEN TO THE RECEIVER, not kept by self, a bonus, an offer code or a model parameter. A USD1 participation fee is separate from the round resources. The instructions shown to participants promise the outcomes of two randomly selected rounds as bonuses, with rounds from both parts equally likely. This is not a promise of exactly one round per part. For a selected round, the participants' start bonuses and relevant allocation outcomes are added to their payments. No selected rounds or realized payments are supplied.

Predict one human monetary allocation in an online experiment with US residents. In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.

Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.

In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.
The displayed response slider is moved with left/right arrow keys and confirmed with Enter. The split changes in USD0.10 increments, from giving nothing to giving the full USD1. Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position. Predict the amount GIVEN TO THE RECEIVER, not kept by self, a bonus, an offer code or a model parameter. A USD1 participation fee is separate from the round resources. The instructions shown to participants promise the outcomes of two randomly selected rounds as bonuses, with rounds from both parts equally likely. This is not a promise of exactly one round per part. For a selected round, the participants' start bonuses and relevant allocation outcomes are added to their payments. No selected rounds or realized payments are supplied.

Predict one human monetary allocation in an online experiment with US residents. In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.
The displayed response slider is moved with left/right arrow keys and confirmed with Enter. The split changes in USD0.10 increments, from giving nothing to giving the full USD1. Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position. Predict the amount GIVEN TO THE RECEIVER, not kept by self, a bonus, an offer code or a model parameter. A USD1 participation fee is separate from the round resources. The instructions shown to participants promise the outcomes of two randomly selected rounds as bonuses, with rounds from both parts equally likely. This is not a promise of exactly one round per part. For a selected round, the participants' start bonuses and relevant allocation outcomes are added to their payments. No selected rounds or realized payments are supplied.

Predict one human monetary allocation in an online experiment with US residents. In Part 1 the participant is the Distributor, deciding how to divide an extra USD1 with a different Receiver each round; the Receiver passively receives that allocation. In Part 2 the same participant is the Proposer, again dividing USD1 with a different Receiver, but this Receiver can later accept or reject the proposed division. The two parts occur in that fixed order. Receivers take part later, so no actual acceptance, rejection or partner response is known at the current decision. A later Receiver session is not an additional action supplied here. There is no communication or repeat encounter with the same partner. The participant enters their own initials for display; in the actual task the other person is labeled Other. Literal initials are not supplied.
Before allocating the extra USD1, both people receive separate start bonuses, each USD0.19, USD0.75 or USD3.00. Both people know these bonuses. The participant's bonus stays constant within a block and changes across blocks; the other person's bonus varies in randomized order. Bonuses are experimental resources, not the person's annual income. If the participant gives x dollars of the extra dollar, they keep 1−x. In Part 1 the round's total amounts are own bonus+1−x and receiver bonus+x. In Part 2 these same amounts apply if the Receiver accepts. If the Receiver rejects, both allocations from the extra dollar are zero; each person retains their own start bonus, as explicitly illustrated in the instructions and task schematic. The participant is not choosing how to transfer the start bonuses themselves.

Its initial handle position is random; the current input does not provide an interpreted starting position.
